group.title: Shades of meaning
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Small or delicate, and not easy to notice.
examples: There is a {subtle} difference between the two words.
wrong: A subtle sound is one so loud that nobody can miss it.

words.meaning: Having more than one possible meaning.
examples: The instructions were {ambiguous}, so we asked for help.
wrong: An ambiguous answer has exactly one clear meaning that nobody can doubt.

words.meaning: Covering all or nearly all parts of something.
examples: The report gives a {comprehensive} view of the market.
wrong: A comprehensive report covers only one small detail and skips the rest.

words.meaning: Certain to happen and impossible to avoid.
examples: Change is {inevitable} in any growing company.
wrong: An inevitable event is one that will certainly never happen.

words.meaning: Existing as a natural and permanent part of something.
examples: Some risk is {inherent} in any new business.
wrong: A risk that is inherent has been added from outside by someone later.

words.meaning: Seeming reasonable and likely to be true.
examples: Her explanation sounded {plausible}.
wrong: A plausible story is one that nobody can believe at all.

words.meaning: Very deep or strong, in feeling or understanding.
examples: The book had a {profound} effect on her.
wrong: A profound idea is shallow and easy to forget.

words.meaning: Important and well known; easy to see.
examples: She is a {prominent} member of the council.
wrong: A prominent person is someone nobody has ever heard of.

words.meaning: Large in amount or importance.
examples: They received a {substantial} amount of money.
wrong: A substantial amount of money is a tiny and unimportant sum.

words.meaning: Only on the surface; not deep or thorough.
examples: He had only a {superficial} knowledge of the subject.
wrong: A superficial study looks at every detail very deeply.

words.meaning: Not certain or fixed; offered with some doubt.
examples: We made a {tentative} plan for next month.
wrong: A tentative plan is one that is final and cannot change.

words.meaning: Complete and careful about every detail.
examples: The police carried out a {thorough} search.
wrong: A thorough check misses most of the details.

words.meaning: Of very little importance.
examples: They argued over a {trivial} matter.
wrong: A trivial matter is something of great importance for everyone.

words.meaning: Not clear or exact.
examples: His answer was too {vague} to be useful.
wrong: A vague answer is one that is precise and exact.

words.meaning: Likely to change quickly and suddenly.
examples: The market is very {volatile} at the moment.
wrong: A volatile market never changes at all.

words.meaning: Logical and clear, with all parts fitting together.
examples: She gave a {coherent} account of the events.
wrong: A coherent argument has parts that do not connect at all.

words.meaning: Stated clearly and openly, with nothing hidden.
examples: The rules are {explicit} about late work.
wrong: An explicit rule is one that is hidden and never stated.

words.meaning: Suggested without being stated directly.
examples: There was an {implicit} threat in his words.
wrong: An implicit message is one that is said directly and loudly.

words.meaning: Very careful and exact.
examples: The test was {rigorous} and fair.
wrong: A rigorous test is careless and sloppy.

words.meaning: Based on chance or choice rather than reason.
examples: The rule seemed {arbitrary} and unfair.
wrong: An arbitrary decision is one that follows a careful and logical reason.

words.meaning: Done on purpose.
examples: It was a {deliberate} attempt to mislead us.
wrong: A deliberate mistake is one made by accident without noticing.

words.meaning: Having many details; complicated.
examples: They made an {elaborate} plan for the party.
wrong: An elaborate plan is simple and has only one step.

words.meaning: Famous for something bad.
examples: The street is {notorious} for its traffic.
wrong: A notorious person is famous for being very kind and good.

words.meaning: No longer used because something better exists.
examples: Typewriters are now {obsolete}.
wrong: An obsolete machine is the newest model that everyone wants.

words.meaning: No longer needed; unnecessary.
examples: Once the new system started, the old weekly report became {redundant}.
wrong: A redundant word is the most important word in a sentence.

words.meaning: Seeming to be everywhere.
examples: Smartphones are now {ubiquitous}.
wrong: A ubiquitous object is one that can be found nowhere.

words.meaning: Able to do many different things.
examples: She is a {versatile} actor who can play any role.
wrong: A versatile tool can do only one single job.

words.meaning: Very careful about small details.
examples: He is {meticulous} about keeping records.
wrong: A meticulous worker is careless about details.

words.meaning: Dealing with problems in a practical way.
examples: We need a {pragmatic} solution, not a perfect one.
wrong: A pragmatic person only follows dreams that cannot work.

words.meaning: Able to recover quickly from difficulties.
examples: Children are often very {resilient}.
wrong: A resilient person is broken by every small problem and never recovers.

words.meaning: Honest and direct, even when it is uncomfortable.
examples: He was {candid} about his mistakes.
wrong: A candid speaker hides the truth and tells lies.

words.meaning: Easy to see or notice.
examples: His red coat was {conspicuous} in the crowd.
wrong: A conspicuous object is hidden and nobody notices it.

words.meaning: Ordinary and not interesting.
examples: She wrote about the {mundane} details of daily life.
wrong: A mundane day is full of strange, exciting events.

words.meaning: Possible and likely to be done.
examples: The plan is {feasible} with the money we have.
wrong: A feasible plan is one that is impossible to carry out.

words.meaning: Producing a lot of money.
examples: He left for a more {lucrative} job.
wrong: A lucrative business loses a great deal of money.

words.meaning: Done without planning or noticing.
examples: It was an {inadvertent} error.
wrong: An inadvertent mistake is made on purpose and with full attention.

words.meaning: Done naturally, without planning.
examples: The crowd gave a {spontaneous} cheer.
wrong: A spontaneous party is one planned carefully months before.

words.meaning: Real and possible to touch or measure.
examples: There is no {tangible} evidence of the plan.
wrong: A tangible result is one that cannot be seen or measured.

words.meaning: Having many small parts that fit together in a complicated way.
examples: The watch has an {intricate} design.
wrong: An intricate pattern is plain, with just one line.

words.meaning: Working with care and effort.
examples: She is a {diligent} student who never misses a class.
wrong: A diligent worker is lazy and avoids work.
